name: Carioca
description: Carioca is an Argentinean Contract Rummy variant similar to Central American Loba. Played over 7 rounds with increasingly difficult contracts. Players try to meld trios (three of a kind) and escaleras (4-card straight flushes) to get rid of all cards. Features wild jokers and the ability to add to other players' melds.

history.origins: Carioca is an Argentinean variant of Contract Rummy, closely related to Central American Loba. The game was documented by Eduardo Valcarcel as played in Argentina. It differs from Loba primarily in having 7 rounds instead of 6.
timeline: Contract Rummy family develops from traditional rummy games
Central American Loba emerges with 6 rounds
Argentinean Carioca variant develops with 7th round
Current: Played throughout Argentina and neighboring regions
history.cultural: Popular in Argentina. The game uses Spanish terminology (trio, escalera, loba). Often played socially in homes and cafes.
history.evolution: Carioca evolved from Loba by adding a 7th round (three escaleras). Scoring differs: jokers=50, aces=20, face cards=10 in Carioca vs jokers=25, aces=14, face cards=face value in Loba.

setup.players: 2-5 players, each playing individually (no partnerships). Deal and play are counter-clockwise.
setup.deck: Two standard 52-card packs plus 4 jokers = 108 cards total. Jokers are wild. Cards rank A-K-Q-J-10-9-8-7-6-5-4-3-2 (Ace high or low in escaleras).
setup.dealing: First dealer chosen at random. Deal passes to the right (counter-clockwise). Rounds 1-6: 11 cards each. Round 7: 12 cards each. One card turned up to start discard pile; remainder forms draw pile.

rules.objective: Get rid of all cards by melding. Lowest cumulative score after 7 rounds wins.
rules.gameplay: 7 rounds with specific contracts: R1=2 trios (6 cards), R2=1 escalera+1 trio (7 cards), R3=2 escaleras (8 cards), R4=3 trios (9 cards), R5=2 trios+1 escalera (10 cards), R6=2 escaleras+1 trio (11 cards), R7=3 escaleras (12 cards). Turn: draw (from discard or draw pile), optionally meld, discard. To meld initially, must have complete contract and put it down at once. After initial meld, can add cards to any existing melds on table (extend trios with same rank, extend escaleras at either end). Cannot create new melds after initial contract. Ace can be high or low in escalera but not both. Jokers wild: max 1 per meld in initial contract, unlimited after. Joker at end of escalera can be moved by tucking in appropriate card. Round ends when player empties hand. Others score cards remaining.
keyRules: Trio = 3 of a kind (suits can match)
Escalera = 4-card straight flush (Ace high or low)
Must have complete contract before initial meld
Can add to any meld on table after initial contract
Jokers wild: 1 per meld initially, unlimited after
Joker at escalera end can be moved by tucking card

strategy.basic: Focus on collecting the required contract cards before melding. Use jokers wisely - they are valuable for scoring but essential for completing difficult contracts.
strategy.intermediate: Time your initial meld - going down early lets you play off on others' melds, but waiting may let you go out in one turn. Watch what cards opponents are collecting. Save high cards for playing on others' melds rather than being stuck with them.
strategy.advanced: Track which cards have been played to estimate what opponents hold. In later rounds, prioritize completing your contract over minimizing score - being stuck with unmelded cards is worse than a few penalty points. Manipulate jokers in escaleras to create more play opportunities.
tips: Jokers are worth 50 points - try not to be stuck with them
Going down early gives more chances to play off cards
Watch opponents' discards for clues about their hands
Escaleras with aces at ends are flexible (A-2-3-4 or J-Q-K-A)
In round 7, you need 12 cards for 3 escaleras - plan accordingly
Adding to opponents' melds helps you but also helps them go out
